Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$, write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use $0\log0=0$, and set the products $q\log\gamma$ and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

In a dominated Bayesian model, a posterior interpretation is available only with the model hypotheses and on fibers with finite positive evidence, as in [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] and [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. In particular, [[def-likelihood-density]] supplies separate likelihood versions but does not assert joint measurability in parameter and data. Supply the single jointly measurable density $\gamma$ explicitly before using Tonelli or a posterior-kernel formula. No quotient is formed at zero or infinite normalizer.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

For all $x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$,
$$\exp((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)\exp x+t\exp y.$$
If $0<t<1$, equality holds exactly when $x=y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

derivations.claim:
Put $\alpha=q_j\mu_j$ and $
u=v\mu_{-j}$. They are probabilities and the law with density $q$ is their product by [F1]–[F3]. A density is positive and finite almost surely under its own probability, since its zero set has mass zero and its infinite set has reference measure zero. Thus $A(x)=\log q_j(x)$ and $B(y)=\log v(y)$ are finite almost surely, and [F8] gives $\log q=A+B$ almost surely. Choose a finite integer $K$ for which $p:=
u(|B|\le K)>0$; such a $K$ exists because those events increase to a full-measure set. On that event $|A|\le|A+B|+K$, so product integration [F2]–[F3] yields $p\int|A|d\alpha\le\int|A+B|d(\alpha\otimes
u)+Kp<\infty$. Interchanging $A$ and $B$ and choosing an analogous positive-probability bounded event proves $\int|B|d
u<\infty$. Hence $H=\int B d
u$ is finite, including $H=0$ for the unit complementary factor.

By [F2] and $Z<\infty$, the marginal $G(x):=\int\gamma(x,y)d\mu_{-j}(y)$ is finite for $\mu_j$-almost every $x$. Fix such an $x$. Under $
u$, define $g(y)=\gamma(x,y)/v(y)$ on $\{0<v<\infty\}$; arbitrary values on its $
u$-null complement do not matter. Then $\int g d
u=\int_{\{0<v<\infty\}}\gamma(x,y)d\mu_{-j}(y)\le G(x)$ by [F3]. In particular $g$ is finite almost surely. Write $L=\log g$, allowing $L=-\infty$ at $g=0$. Its positive part is integrable since $\log^+g\le g$, and the defined expected-log convention and integrability of $B$ give $\int Ld
u=h_j(x)-H$ in the extended sense; in particular $h_j(x)$ cannot equal $+\infty$.

Let $L_n=\max(L,-n)$. Its negative part is bounded and its positive part is integrable by step 2.1, so $L_n$ is integrable. Also $e^{L_n}=\max(g,e^{-n})\le g+1$ is integrable. Apply [F4] with the convex exponential [F5] to obtain $\exp(\int L_n d
u)\le\int e^{L_n}d
u$. The negative parts increase to $L^-$, so [F6] gives $\int L_n d
u\downarrow\int Ld
u$, possibly $-\infty$. By [F7], the right side tends to $\int g d
u$, with domination $g+1$; continuity of the exponential and $e^{-\infty}=0$ therefore give $\exp(h_j(x)-H)\le\int g d
u\le G(x)$.

The inequality in step 2.2 holds for $\mu_j$-almost every $x$. Multiply it by $e^H$ and integrate using [F2] to obtain $c_j\le e^H\int Gd\mu_j=e^HZ<\infty$. Since $h_j$ is finite $\alpha$-almost surely, $e^{h_j}>0$ on an $\alpha$-full measurable set. If $c_j=0$, [F9] would make this set $\mu_j$-null, hence $\alpha$-null by [F3], contradicting $\alpha(\Omega_j)=1$. Thus $c_j>0$. This does not prove admissibility of the normalized replacement, which remains a separate requirement.

**Inputs:** A finite number $m\ge1$ of sigma-finite factor reference spaces $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$, their product reference measure $\mu$, a measurable target $\gamma$ with finite positive normalizer, an admissible initial mean-field density $q=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j$, and a finite sweep count $N\ge0$.

**Output:** The current admissible product density after at most $N$ full sweeps, together with a status indicating whether the requested sweeps completed or a coordinate update was unavailable.

For each sweep $t=1,\ldots,N$, visit coordinates in the fixed order $j=1,\ldots,m$. At coordinate $j$, keep $q_{-j}:=\prod_{k\ne j}q_k$ fixed; for $m=1$, the empty product reference space is a singleton with unit measure $\mu_{-j}$ and its density is $1$. Form the conditional log expectation
$$h_j(z_j):=\int_{\prod_{k\ne j}\Omega_k}\log\gamma(z_j,z_{-j})q_{-j}(z_{-j})\,d\mu_{-j}(z_{-j}).$$
Use this signed integral only when it is defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity and has a measurable extended-real version; require it to be finite for current $q_j$-almost every $z_j$. Set
$$c_j:=\int_{\Omega_j}e^{h_j(z_j)}\,\mu_j(dz_j).$$
If $0<c_j<\infty$ and the normalized density $q_j^*(z_j):=e^{h_j(z_j)}/c_j$ makes $q_j^*q_{-j}$ an admissible member of the mean-field family, replace $q_j$ by $q_j^*$. Otherwise stop and return the current density with status “coordinate update unavailable.”

The algorithm performs only the requested finite sweeps. It makes no convergence, stationary-point, global-optimum, calibration, or approximation-error claim. A separate theorem on this page proves exact coordinate monotonicity under these conditions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

derivations.claim:
Put $r_n=2^{-n}$, $b_n=-2\log(n+1)$, $a_n=-(1-r_n)b_n/r_n=2(2^n-1)\log(n+1)>0$, and $w_m=e^{-2a_m}$. Define $\gamma(n,m)=e^{a_n}$ when $m=n$ and $\gamma(n,m)=e^{b_n}=(n+1)^{-2}$ otherwise. By [F3],
$Z=\sum_m e^{-2a_m}\left(e^{a_m}+\sum_{n\ne m}(n+1)^{-2}\right)$. For every $m$, $a_m\ge2\log(m+1)>0$, so $e^{-a_m}\le(m+1)^{-2}$. Also $\sum_n(n+1)^{-2}<\infty$ because $(n+1)^{-2}\le[n(n+1)]^{-1}=1/n-1/(n+1)$. Hence $0<Z\le\sum_m e^{-a_m}+\left(\sum_m e^{-2a_m}\right)\left(\sum_n(n+1)^{-2}\right)<\infty$.

Give the $X$-factor masses $q_X(n)=r_n$ and the $Y$-factor density $q_Y(m)=r_m/w_m$ relative to $\mu_Y$. Each factor has total mass $\sum_n r_n=1$, so $q(n,m)=r_nr_m/w_m$ is a product probability density by [F3]. It is positive wherever $\gamma$ is positive, so it satisfies the support condition in [F1].

For fixed $n$, the expectation of $\log\gamma(n,Y)$ under $q_Y$ is $r_na_n+(1-r_n)b_n=0$. Its absolute expectation is $r_na_n+(1-r_n)|b_n|=2(1-r_n)|b_n|\le4\log(n+1)$. Therefore $\int q|\log\gamma|d\mu\le4\sum_n2^{-n}\log(n+1)<\infty$. For $n\ge1$, [F4] and [F5] give $\log(n+1)=\int_1^{n+1}dt/t\le n$, since $0<1/t\le1$ on $[1,n+1]$. Also, for $n\ge4$ one has $n\le2^{n/2}$ by induction, so $n2^{-n}\le2^{-n/2}$ and the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series.

For $m\ge1$, induction gives $2^m-1\ge m$, and monotonicity of the logarithm gives $\log(m+1)\ge\log2>0$. Hence $a_m=2(2^m-1)\log(m+1)\ge2m\log2\ge(m+1)\log2$. On the row $n=1$, $\log q(1,m)=-(m+1)\log2+2a_m\ge a_m$. Its contribution to the nonnegative entropy integral is therefore at least $r_1\sum_m r_ma_m$. But $r_ma_m=2(1-2^{-m})\log(m+1)\ge\log2$ for every $m\ge1$, so that series diverges. By [F3], $\int q|\log q|d\mu=\infty$, and [F1] shows that $q$ is not admissible.

For the $X$-coordinate update with $q_Y$ fixed, step 3.1 gives $h(n)=E_{q_Y}\log\gamma(n,Y)=0$ for every $n$. Therefore the update normalizer in [F2] is $\sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{h(n)}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty1=\infty$. Thus finite evidence, support and finite pointwise expected log do not suffice: no normalized coordinate factor exists, and step 4.1 identifies the failed admissibility hypothesis.

Let $\mu,\gamma,Z,\pi,q$ satisfy [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]], and put $Q=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi=\pi\,\mu$. The choice-free density-ratio identity
$$\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu$$
holds, with the ratio integrand set to zero where $q=0$. Under AC, the final integral is the library reverse divergence $D(Q\|\Pi)$ and is nonnegative. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix any $c\in\mathbb R$. By the onto clause of [F5], choose $a>0$ with $\log a=c$. Define $\gamma_c=a\gamma$. Homogeneity [F4] gives $Z_c=\int\gamma_c d\mu=aZ$, so $\pi_c=\gamma_c/Z_c=\pi$ and both $Q$ and $\Pi$ remain unchanged. Since $\pi_c=\pi$, the support condition in [F1] is unchanged. On the q-support, $|\log\gamma_c|\le|\log\gamma|+|c|$, so the logarithmic integrability condition remains finite.

On the q-support the logarithm product law [F5] gives $\log\gamma_c=\log\gamma+c$. Using [F2], $\operatorname{ELBO}_c(q)=\int q(\log\gamma+c-\log q)d\mu=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+c$. Since $c$ is arbitrary, the absolute ELBO can be made arbitrarily large while $Q$, $\Pi$, and any fixed discrepancy between them stay unchanged.

Under [A1], the decomposition [F3] gives $\log Z-\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=D(Q\|\Pi)$. Without control of $\log Z$, a separate calibration theorem, or another posterior-discrepancy bound, the absolute ELBO alone supplies no calibration guarantee.
